analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for oil spill cleanup and liability costs.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a vote, a hearing, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the tax code so oil companies could no longer deduct the cost of cleaning up oil spills or paying damage claims from their taxable income. Normally those costs work like any business expense: a company that spills oil deducts the cleanup bill and ordinary taxpayers effectively cover a share of it. The bill would apply to spills from vessels carrying the taxpayer's oil, starting with costs incurred after December 31, 1988.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would stop indirectly subsidizing oil spill cleanup — under the standard corporate tax rate of the era, the deduction let a spilling company shift roughly a third of its cleanup and liability costs onto the federal treasury. Coastal communities and fishermen would also gain from a stronger financial incentive to prevent spills in the first place.

how_it_helps.text: Ends the practice of letting companies write off oil spill cleanup and damage costs as ordinary business expenses, so the company that caused the spill bears the full cost instead of sharing it with federal taxpayers through a smaller tax bill.
Covers both removal costs and liability for damages — the full financial fallout of a spill, not just the physical cleanup.
Creates a stronger financial incentive for oil shippers to prevent spills, since a spill could no longer be softened by a tax deduction.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies and tanker operators transporting petroleum on navigable waters, who would pay the full after-tax cost of any spill cleanup and damage claims rather than deducting them — effectively a penalty layered on top of existing liability, at a rate equal to the corporate tax rate they would otherwise have saved.

drawbacks.text: It breaks from a basic principle of the tax code: businesses deduct the ordinary costs of doing business, and opponents of this approach argue that forcing a company to pay cleanup costs with after-tax dollars amounts to a back-door fine on top of whatever civil and criminal liability already applies — a penalty set by the tax-writing committees rather than by courts or environmental agencies.

The denial would be retroactive, applying to costs incurred after December 31, 1988 in taxable years ending after that date — meaning companies facing spills already underway when the bill was introduced would face the higher cost with no notice.
The bill is narrow: it covers only oil discharged from a vessel transporting oil by or for the taxpayer, leaving spills from pipelines, facilities, and other sources under the normal deduction rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face this is a clean polluter-pays measure: it removes a taxpayer subsidy for the exact costs a company's own actions create. The honest cost is that it does so through the tax code rather than by raising liability limits or penalties directly, it reaches only a slice of potential spill sources, and its retroactive start date is hard to defend. Whether denying the deduction is sound policy or double punishment is a fair argument — but the bill never got far enough for that argument to happen.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Douglas Applegate introduced the bill on April 25, 1989, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax law.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The Ways and Means Committee took no further action — no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies and tanker operators kept the ability to deduct spill cleanup and damage costs from their taxes, and federal taxpayers continued to pick up a share of those costs.

for.name: Douglas Applegate
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to deny tax deductions for oil spill cleanup and damage costs.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: The committee with jurisdiction over tax law (chaired by Dan Rostenkowski, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no recorded opposition, so no partisan split can be measured; the bill had one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of any party.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to deduct spill cleanup and damage costs, raising the after-tax price of every spill by roughly the corporate tax rate — about a third of the bill at the era's rates. Their interest in keeping the deduction ran directly against taxpayers, who foot the other portion of every cleanup.
